In [[mathematics]], in particular in [[measure theory]], an '''inner measure''' is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] on the [[power set]] of a given [[Set (mathematics)|set]], with values in the [[Extended real line|extended real numbers]], satisfying some technical conditions. Intuitively, the inner measure of a set is a lower bound of the size of that set.

== Definition ==

An inner measure is a [[set function]]
<math display=block>\varphi : 2^X \to [0, \infty],</math>
defined on all [[subset]]s of a set <math>X,</math> that satisfies the following conditions:

* Null empty set: The [[empty set]] has zero inner measure (''see also: [[measure zero]]''); that is, <math display=block>\varphi(\varnothing) = 0</math>
* [[Superadditivity|Superadditive]]: For any [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] sets <math>A</math> and <math>B,</math> <math display=block>\varphi(A \cup B) \geq \varphi(A) + \varphi(B).</math>
* Limits of decreasing towers: For any [[sequence]] <math>A_1, A_2, \ldots</math> of sets such that <math> A_j \supseteq A_{j+1}</math> for each <math>j</math> and <math>\varphi(A_1) < \infty</math> <math display=block>\varphi \left(\bigcap_{j=1}^\infty A_j\right) = \lim_{j \to \infty} \varphi(A_j)</math>
* If the measure is not finite, that is, if there exist sets <math>A</math> with <math>\varphi(A) = \infty</math>, then this infinity must be approached. More precisely, if <math>\varphi(A) = \infty</math> for a set <math>A</math> then for every positive [[real number]] <math>r,</math> there exists some <math>B \subseteq A</math> such that <math display=block>r \leq \varphi(B) < \infty.</math>

== The inner measure induced by a measure ==

Let <math>\Sigma</math> be a [[σ-algebra]] over a set <math>X</math> and <math>\mu</math> be a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] on <math>\Sigma.</math> 
Then the inner measure <math>\mu_*</math> induced by <math>\mu</math> is defined by
<math display=block>\mu_*(T) = \sup\{\mu(S) : S \in \Sigma \text{ and } S \subseteq T\}.</math>

Essentially <math>\mu_*</math> gives a lower bound of the size of any set by ensuring it is at least as big as the <math>\mu</math>-measure of any of its <math>\Sigma</math>-measurable subsets. Even though the set function <math>\mu_*</math> is usually not a measure, <math>\mu_*</math> shares the following properties with measures:
# <math>\mu_*(\varnothing) = 0,</math>
# <math>\mu_*</math> is non-negative,
# If <math>E \subseteq F</math> then <math>\mu_*(E) \leq \mu_*(F).</math>

== Measure completion ==
{{main|Complete measure}}

Induced inner measures are often used in combination with [[outer measure]]s to extend a measure to a larger σ-algebra. If <math>\mu</math> is a finite measure defined on a [[σ-algebra]] <math>\Sigma</math> over <math>X</math> and <math>\mu^*</math> and <math>\mu_*</math> are corresponding induced outer and inner measures, then the sets <math>T \in 2^X</math> such that <math>\mu_*(T) = \mu^*(T)</math> form a σ-algebra <math style="vertical-align:0%;">\hat \Sigma</math> with <math style="vertical-align:-15%;">\Sigma\subseteq\hat\Sigma</math>.<ref>Halmos 1950, § 14, Theorem F</ref>  
The set function <math>\hat\mu</math> defined by
<math display=block>\hat\mu(T) = \mu^*(T) = \mu_*(T)</math>
for all <math style="vertical-align:0%;">T \in \hat \Sigma</math> is a measure on <math style="vertical-align:0%;">\hat \Sigma</math> known as the completion of <math>\mu.</math>
